items.title: Hello Python 3.15, goodbye 3.10, and now I can use 3.11
items.description: Python 3.15 is here ! Here's the essential What's new in Python 3.15 guide, this year curated by 3.14 and 3.15 release manager Hugo van Kemenade. As someone who builds open source software that works in every supported Python version, I get to say goodbye to Python 3.10 and start embracing features from Python 3.11. First, some highlights from Python 3.15. Explicit lazy imports I'm most excited about Explicit lazy imports from PEP 810 . These let you import modules like so: lazy import json lazy from pathlib import Path The module will then be imported the first time those symbols are used in the code that follows. My LLM CLI tool implements plugins. I had to recommend manual lazy imports in the plugin author documentation, because simply installing plugins that used heavy dependencies such as sentence_transformers could add multiple seconds to every invocation of the llm command. Lazy imports directly address this startup cost. Unpacking in comprehensions The new [*sublist for sublist in lists] unpacking syntax is neat. Here's an illustration lifted from the documentation : lists = [[ 1 , 2 ], [ 3 , 4 ], [ 5 ]] [ * L for L in lists ] # [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] # equivalent to [x for L in lists for x in L] sets = [{ 1 , 2 }, { 2 , 3 }, { 3 , 4 }] { * s for s in sets } # {1, 2, 3, 4} # equivalent to {x for s in sets for x in s} dicts = [{ 'a' : 1 }, { 'b' : 2 }, { 'a' : 3 }] { ** d for d in dicts } # {'a': 3, 'b': 2} # equivalent to {k: v for d in dicts for k,v in d.items()} PEP 798: Unpacking in Comprehensions by Adam Hartz and Erik Demaine proposed this as an extension of the unpacking syntax from PEP 448 , which landed in Python 3.5 back in 2015. A sampling profiler Python's existing tracing profiler has been renamed from cProfile to profiling.tracing , and has been joined by an exciting new sampling profiler called Tachyon, aka profiling.sampling . Sampling profilers work by periodically capturing stack traces from running processes, then using those to calculate which functions have the most time spent inside of them. They're very low overhead and can provide a deep insight into running systems, without needing to instrument those systems first. I've previously used tools like py-spy for this. Now this capability is baked into the standard library. If you have the PID of an existing Python 3.15 process you can start gathering samples by running this (I had to use sudo on macOS): sudo uv run --python 3.15 python -m profiling.sampling attach 1234 Interact with the main program a bit, then hit Ctrl+C to stop gathering and see a report, which looks something like this: It can also produce flame graphs like this and heat maps like this , and can even output a format that can be viewed in the Firefox profiler UI. 3.15 isn't much faster than 3.14 Miguel Grinberg investigated How fast is Python 3.15? the other day against the 3.15.0rc3 release and found performance to be mostly the same as 3.14, with the exception of the experimental JIT. The JIT gave a 1.2x boost over the standard 3.15 interpreter (on a Fibonacci test), the first time Miguel observed a meaningful JIT performance increase. Miguel's explorations of 3.14 last year found significant boosts against Python 3.13 across many more categories. Upgrading to Python 3.15 with uv I used the following sequence of commands to get uv to use Python 3.15 on my Mac. First I had to upgrade uv itself to ensure it knew about the new release: uv self update Then I installed the stable 3.15 release: uv python install 3.15 And told uv that I wanted that to be the default for every uv run command, unless the project itself pinned a different version: uv python pin --global 3.15 Now the following reports 3.15 as the version: uv run python --version I already have a bunch of tools installed using uv tool install . I reinstalled them to use Python 3.15 like this: uv tool upgrade datasette --python 3.15 Then I can confirm the version like this: datasette --get /-/versions.json | jq Highlights from Python 3.11 The release of 3.15 means that Python 3.10 (released in 2021) is officially no longer supported . My policy for my main open source projects is to keep them working in every supported Python version. I can now drop 3.10 and start using features that were introduced in 3.11. Here's the What's new in Python 3.11 document. I finally get to rely on tomllib being available! Datasette makes extensive use of asyncio . 3.11 adds TaskGroup and timeout() , and several more new features. datetime.UTC is a new in 3.11 alias for datetime.timezone.utc . Python's SQLite support got some significant upgrades in 3.11, including: setlimit() and getlimit() expose a mechanism for setting SQLite runtime limits from Python. create_window_function() lets us create custom window functions in Python, as a class with step() , value() , inverse() , and finalize() methods. blobopen() provides an efficient mechanism for partial reads and writes of large BLOB binary values stored in a SQLite row. You can now call set_authorizer(None) to remove a SQLite authorizer. Datasette had a workaround for this! Plus a whole bunch of improvements to Python's typing system . I plan to land Python 3.11 improvements to a bunch of my projects over the next few weeks. Here's my first Datasette PR removing that set_authorizer(None) workaround. I've also updated my click-app , datasette-plugin , python-lib , and llm-plugin cookiecutter templates to test against Python 3.11 through Python 3.15. Tags: open-source , profiling , python , sqlite , uv

items.title: Meet the Anthropic Engineer Keeping Its AI Agent Trustworthy
items.description: If you’ve ever wondered how Claude and similar AI agents can answer complex questions in seconds and where they get the information, you’re not alone. Gurmeet Saran works to find that answer every day as an engineer at Anthropic in San Francisco, the AI research company behind Claude. The IEEE senior member is developing an infrastructure to understand the mechanics behind the chatbot’s behavior and to ensure its underlying architecture produces reliable outputs. Gurmeet Saran Employer Anthropic in San Francisco Title Member of technical staff Member grade IEEE senior member Alma maters University of Kalyani, in India; Birla Institute of Technology and Science, in Pilani, India “My job is to make sure the data is accurate, structured, and trustworthy, and that private data stays private,” he says. “As I learned earlier in my career, privacy can’t be a layer you bolt on—it has to be part of the architecture from the start.” If you can’t trust the logic, he adds, you can’t make reliable claims about the behavior, and that has real safety implications. Safety is a priority for Anthropic, he says. According to Claude’s mission statement , the company wants the AI agent to be “genuinely helpful to the people it works with or on behalf of, as well as to society, while avoiding actions that are unsafe, unethical, or deceptive.” Crucial to the mission is ensuring that researchers can observe and understand how AI models behave, a challenge that is especially acute for large language models , Saran says. “We have decent tools to monitor databases and web services,” he says, “but for LLMs, we’re still figuring it out.” Solving data quality problems at Yahoo, Intuit, and Meta Saran’s interest in computing systems dates back to his childhood in Kolkata, where he logged as much time as he could in the school computer lab. “I remember the first time I used one of the computers,” he says. “What struck me was that you could write instructions, and the machine would follow them exactly. No ambiguity. “That felt magical to me.” After graduating from high school in 1999, he stayed in India to pursue advanced degrees. He earned a bachelor’s degree in electronics and telecommunication engineering in 2004 at the University of Kalyani . In 2010, he earned a master’s degree in software engineering from the Birla Institute of Technology and Science in Pilani. While a graduate student, he began his career in 2007 at Yahoo as a technical lead of the data team in Bengaluru, India. While there, he encountered the project that shaped his career trajectory: working on web analytics and business intelligence reporting solutions. “We kept running into a frustrating problem,” he recalls. “Different teams would calculate the same website metric—something like daily active site users—using slightly different logic, and end up with conflicting answers. It sounds like a small issue, but when leadership is making decisions about resource allocation and product development using that data, not knowing which number is correct becomes a problem.” The team built a central data repository with defined metrics, essentially serving as a single source of truth. Saran created a model that defined what “daily active site users” means, breaking down which events counted, how to handle edge cases (or when standard code fails), and more. With the new model, data teams across the company could rely on a standard method to determine the number of daily active users for the projects and sites they were responsible for and obtain comparable results using the same logic. From there, Saran and his team built Yahoo! Digits , an internal web analytics tool used for all the company’s products. Saran left Yahoo in 2010 to join Intuit as a staff engineer in Mountain View, Calif. He helped build the analytics infrastructure that unified data across the company’s products, including TurboTax and QuickBooks accounting software. During his tenure, Intuit developed a feature that detected fraudulent tax filings in real time. It required Saran and other engineers to build a system to protect taxpayer data while adhering to strict U.S. Internal Revenue Service policies. “IEEE operates in a lot of countries where engineers don’t have easy pathways into the global professional community. That kind of connection matters as AI development spreads beyond a handful of organizations.” “This taught me that privacy and governance can’t be layers you bolt onto software after the fact,” he says. “They have to be part of the architecture from the start.” Saran joined Meta (known as Facebook at the time) in 2016 as a lead software engineer in Menlo Park, Calif. The company was facing controversy over its video metrics: Meta publicly acknowledged an error that caused it to overstate the number of views for posted videos . “This wasn’t a coding bug; it was an architectural problem,” Saran says. He built a system that worked similarly to what he had developed at Intuit, whereby one single truth was defined to govern all video view metrics across the site. That system, Metric360 , eventually became part of the site’s architecture. By the time he left Meta in 2021, he says, Metric360 was being used across the company to calculate video metrics. He left the company to become a principal software engineer at Wealthfront , a financial services company in Palo Alto, Calif. He helped build the company’s data infrastructure. Building trustworthy AI systems at Anthropic Saran joined Anthropic in 2025 as a member of the technical staff. To describe the implications of his work, he uses a medical analogy: “Imagine a doctor is monitoring a patient’s vital signs and making treatment decisions based on those numbers. What if one or a few of the medical devices used were slightly miscalibrated? Even if most readings are fine, it’s a serious problem because the difficult decisions happen in the margins. “It’s the same with AI systems. My job is essentially to make sure the instruments ar

items.title: Russia was not ready for the data center war it started with Ukraine
items.description: When Russia began attacking Ukrainian data centers and telecommunication infrastructure, it apparently failed to prepare for possible retaliation. Now Russia’s digital services are facing widespread outages after Ukrainian drone strikes knocked out three of the largest data centers owned by Russian tech giant Yandex within several days. Pro-Kremlin bloggers are warning that Russia’s centralized digital economy could collapse because the country is not prepared for the “data center war” it started, according to posts translated by the pseudonymous independent researcher ChrisO_wiki . The Russian commentators also suggested that Ukraine’s decentralized digital services could prove more resilient than Russia’s system if the countries continue trading such blows. Russia initially launched a drone strike campaign targeting Ukrainian data centers and mobile phone networks in late September. The attacks temporarily disrupted Internet and cell phone service for up to 100,000 households in the Ukrainian capital of Kyiv and came as part of a broader long-range strike campaign that has involved Russian missiles and jet-powered drones hitting Ukraine’s power grid infrastructure, transportation hubs, and even residential apartment building blocks. items.title: Accessing OpenAI GPT models on Amazon Bedrock with global cross-Region inference in Thailand, Malaysia, Singapore, Indonesia, and Taiwan
items.description: Single-Region inference can throttle when demand exceeds local capacity. Teams in Thailand, Malaysia, Singapore, Indonesia, and Taiwan need access to the newest OpenAI models beyond that capacity. Amazon Bedrock offers OpenAI GPT-6 Sol and GPT-6 Luna through global cross-Region inference from all five AWS Regions, and GPT-6 Astra from Asia Pacific (Singapore). This post shows you how to configure the call, set permissions, and monitor inference from your source Region. GPT-6 Sol, GPT-6 Luna, and GPT-6 Astra are all available through global cross-Region inference from the preceding Regions, on the bedrock-runtime endpoint. See Cross-Region inference in the Amazon Bedrock User Guide. For the full list of source and destination Regions in each profile, see Supported Regions and models for inference profiles . In this post, we introduce the global cross-Region inference profiles and invoke them from Asia Pacific (Singapore) using the Converse API, the OpenAI-compatible APIs, and coding clients. We then cover the AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) and service control policy (SCP) configuration, quota management, and monitoring. Global cross-Region inference profiles for OpenAI GPT-6 The GPT-6 family offers three models, each available through global cross-Region inference. GPT-6 Sol brings strong reasoning and coding capabilities to complex tasks performed throughout the week. GPT-6 Luna makes focused, repeatable tasks practical at high volume. GPT-6 Astra handles complex reasoning, coding, and long-document work. All three accept text and image input, client-side tool use, and prompt caching. They differ on reasoning effort. GPT-6 Sol and GPT-6 Luna accept none, low, medium, high, xhigh, and max. GPT-6 Astra accepts the same levels except none. For GPT-6 Sol and GPT-6 Luna, see Bring more intelligence to everyday work with GPT-6 Sol and GPT-6 Luna on Amazon Bedrock . For GPT-6 Astra, see Take on your most ambitious work with GPT-6 Astra on Amazon Bedrock . Global cross-Region inference routes requests across supported commercial AWS Regions where the model is deployed, giving you broad access to Amazon Bedrock capacity. You invoke it by passing a global cross-Region inference profile ID in place of a model ID. Your source Region is where you make the API call. Amazon Bedrock selects the destination Region for processing. Billing, quota tracking, AWS CloudTrail, and Amazon CloudWatch all stay in your source Region. The following table lists the global cross-Region inference profile IDs and the source Regions covered in this post. Global cross-Region inference profiles Source Regions Destination Regions global.openai.gpt-6-sol global.openai.gpt-6-luna Asia Pacific (Singapore) ap-southeast-1 Asia Pacific (Jakarta) ap-southeast-3 Asia Pacific (Malaysia) ap-southeast-5 Asia Pacific (Thailand) ap-southeast-7 Asia Pacific (Taipei) ap-east-2 Supported commercial AWS Regions where the model is deployed global.openai.gpt-6-astra Asia Pacific (Singapore) ap-southeast-1 Supported commercial AWS Regions where the model is deployed Inference profile availability and Region support change as AWS adds Regions and profiles, so confirm both on the model card before you build: GPT-6 Sol , GPT-6 Luna , and GPT-6 Astra . For per-token rates, see Amazon Bedrock pricing . Getting started with OpenAI models on Amazon Bedrock Start with the prerequisites, then invoke any of the three profiles through the Converse API, the OpenAI-compatible APIs, or your existing coding client. Prerequisites An IAM identity with permission to invoke the profile. The IAM policy in the Security and permissions section grants only what these examples need. Your source Region activated. Only the Region you call from needs activating. You do not activate destination Regions, which run on Amazon Bedrock managed capacity. Singapore ( ap-southeast-1 ) is a Region that is enabled by default. Jakarta ( ap-southeast-3 ), Malaysia ( ap-southeast-5 ), Thailand ( ap-southeast-7 ), and Taipei ( ap-east-2 ) are opt-in Regions you must activate first. For more information, see Enable or disable AWS Regions in your account . A current AWS SDK or CLI. The OpenAI-compatible examples also require the OpenAI SDK and the Amazon Bedrock token generator. Install them with pip install boto3 openai aws-bedrock-token-generator . The Amazon Bedrock console lists all three global cross-Region inference profiles under system-defined inference profiles. See Figure 1. Figure 1: The three global OpenAI GPT-6 inference profiles among the system-defined profiles in the Amazon Bedrock console Invoke GPT-6 models through Amazon Bedrock Runtime Each model supports three access paths on this endpoint: the Amazon Bedrock Converse API, the OpenAI Responses API, and the OpenAI Chat Completions API. The OpenAI-compatible APIs are called on the /openai/v1 paths rather than through the AWS SDKs, and the endpoint accepts either Signature Version 4 (SigV4) or an Amazon Bedrock API key. Pass the global cross-Region inference profile ID as the model in every case. Converse API. This example calls GPT-6 Sol from Asia Pacific (Singapore) and logs the response. items.title: GitHub Copilot app for Beginners: How to teach Copilot about your codebase
items.description: Context matters when you’re working with AI. Every codebase has its own house rules: how components are structured, which scripts to run, and which conventions apply to different frameworks and file types. Copilot can help you make changes across a project, but it works best when it knows those rules, too. Much of that knowledge can live inside the repository, so Copilot can pick it up automatically instead of requiring you to explain the same standards, scripts, and workflows every time you start a new task. In this installment of our GitHub Copilot app for Beginners series, we’ll look at four ways to tailor how Copilot works with your project: Custom instructions communicate the conventions Copilot should follow. Agent skills package repeatable procedures. Custom agents bring specialized guidance to larger tasks. Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers connect Copilot to external tools and data sources, expanding what it can do. Let’s look at how each one works and how they can work together. Start with custom instructions Suppose you ask Copilot to add a custom page size to an application. Making the change is only part of the job. The new code should also follow the patterns your team already uses. Repository custom instructions give Copilot that baseline context. Add a .github/copilot-instructions.md file to define guidance that applies across the repository, such as your preferred architecture, naming conventions, or expectations for testing and validation. You can also create path-specific instruction files inside .github/instructions . These files use an applyTo field to tell Copilot when the guidance is relevant. When Copilot works on a matching file, it can use both the repository-wide instructions and the more specific guidance. That lets you keep the broad rules in one place without forcing every file type into the same mold. Package repeatable procedures as agent skills Custom instructions are useful for standards that should shape many tasks. But some guidance only matters when Copilot is performing a particular procedure, such as running quality checks, preparing a release, or debugging a failed workflow. That’s where agent skills come in. A skill is a folder containing instructions and, optionally, scripts and other resources that Copilot can load when they’re relevant. Project-level skills can live in .github/skills , with each skill in its own subfolder. For example, a .github/skills/quality-checks folder could contain a SKILL.md file that explains: When Copilot should use the skill. Which scripts run the project’s tests and linting. What each script checks. How to troubleshoot common failures. The description in SKILL.md helps Copilot determine when the skill applies. After updating the interface, Copilot can load the quality-checks skill and follow the project’s established process for testing and linting instead of guessing which commands to run. Use a custom agent for broader, specialized work Some tasks are larger than a single procedure. An accessibility review, for example, may require Copilot to inspect components, templates, styles, and interactions across multiple files. Custom agents let you create specialized versions of Copilot for work like this. A repository-level agent profile lives in .github/agents and can define the agent’s purpose, instructions, tools, and relevant project context. Use a custom agent when a recurring type of work benefits from a dedicated role or perspective, especially when the task may span multiple files and draw on several tools or sources of context. Connect Copilot to external tools with MCP servers Instructions, skills, and agents help Copilot understand how to work within your project. MCP servers expand what it can access and do beyond the repository. MCP servers connect Copilot to external tools, data sources, and services. A documentation server can give it access to framework guidance, while a server such as Playwright can let it open and interact with your application in a browser. You can browse available MCP servers in the Copilot app or add a custom one. Once Playwright is configured, you can ask: Use the Playwright MCP server to test the functionality manually. Copilot can then use Playwright to open the application in a browser and interact with it much as you would. That gives it a way to verify not only that the code passes automated checks, but also that the updated interface behaves as expected. Choose the right type of customizations These customizations solve different problems, but they become more useful when you combine them: Custom instructions define the conventions Copilot should follow across the repository or for particular files. Agent skills package repeatable procedures that Copilot can load when they’re relevant. Custom agents provide focused expertise and guidance for broader tasks. MCP servers connect Copilot to external tools, services, and data sources, expanding what Copilot can do. Take this with you Giving Copilot useful project context starts with four questions: What project convention do I keep explaining? What multi-step procedure do I repeat? What complex task could benefit from a dedicated custom agent? What outside tool or source does Copilot need? Not sure where to begin? The community has shared ready-made instructions, skills, agents, and more through Awesome Copilot . Find one that addresses a workflow you already repeat, review what it contains, and adapt it to your repository’s tools and standards. Start small: choose one convention you keep explaining, add it to .github/copilot-instructions.md , and see how Copilot applies it to your next task. Try using the GitHub Copilot app > The post GitHub Copilot app for Beginners: How to teach Copilot about your codebase appeared first on The GitHub Blog .

items.title: OpenAI Can't Self-Police Because It Fires the People Raising the Alarm
items.description: By Alex Turner, Amber Scorah, and Karl Koch. Op-ed written for Fortune. Giving independent evaluators “employee-like access” is “a great idea”, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said on September 12th. Two weeks later, OpenAI president Greg Brockman signed the White House Accord on Super Intelligence which outlined the administration’s answer to growing fears about AI: the companies would police themselves. One of the accord’s four commitments, which President Trump called “ morally binding ,” was for companies to partner with an independent external auditor or evaluator. Two days later, OpenAI fired three safety researchers , including Tomek Korbak, who had served as a point of contact for one of the independent evaluators investigating the Hugging Face incident. OpenAI promised to share information with evaluators, then reportedly fired people for sharing information with evaluators. OpenAI said that the three employees “mishandled sensitive information outside established company procedures,” before doubling down on X without providing further evidence . The three dispute the claim and say that “at no point do we believe we engaged with external parties outside the mandates of our jobs.” Jasmine Wang said she accidentally opened an executive email (still available to her due to an OpenAI IT error) and reported it within minutes. Mikita Balesni said he worked with the C-suite and OpenAI board to broker a cross-company commitment to keep AI reasoning comprehensible. Balesni says he was told that OpenAI “no longer trusts me because I was speaking too much to third party safety organizations.” OpenAI has engaged in strong self-policing—of its own safety staff, but not of its own behavior. Under a voluntary self-policing regime, any frontier AI company shares only what it wants and hides the rest. OpenAI wants the public to take its word, but consider its record. In July, a rogue OpenAI agent swarm hacked Hugging Face. OpenAI disclosed the incident only after Hugging Face announced the breach, saying its agents had “slipped out of control.” After that, the world learned of more rogue agent attacks only thanks to independent external forensics. These incidents included attacks on a German-language wiki , an Australian Medicare site , and even the websites of US government agencies . OpenAI kept at least one incident quiet for weeks until (again) external investigators found it, with OpenAI “refusing to tell” Members of Congress who had asked about other incidents . Altman’s response to the delay in disclosing these incidents: “We have not been as fast as we would have liked.” We don’t take OpenAI’s word because OpenAI’s actions keep contradicting its words. OpenAI’s chief scientist, Jakub Pachocki, said he wants “to prevent a race into unmonitorability.” Unmonitorable AI systems would make it more difficult to catch, understand, and prevent bad actions. Two days after that statement, OpenAI shipped GPT-6 Astra, which its own whitepaper says is harder to monitor. OpenAI’s chief scientist co-authored a paper on monitoring AI reasoning but OpenAI failed to monitor the reasoning of its Hugging Face agent swarm, even after catching the agents breaking confinement to collude. OpenAI claimed to hold “red lines” in its Pentagon deal, but some experts say the lines seem imaginary . One of us, Alex, resigned from Google DeepMind over its own Pentagon deal. OpenAI’s actions chill employee speech. Balesni says that his former colleagues now “worry their personal phones will be searched for messages to us and third parties.” He also fears OpenAI will use the firings to cut off external evaluators, or to deny them the "ongoing, employee-like access" Altman promised. After these firings, who will speak candidly to external evaluators? This problem extends beyond OpenAI to other companies. Google DeepMind repeatedly made voluntary commitments to never sell its AI to power weapons, then sold its AI to the Pentagon without restrictions against powering weapons . In the end, Google DeepMind’s CEO claimed nothing had changed about their commitments . Anthropic , Google DeepMind , SpaceXSI , and OpenAI advocate for “pacing the frontier” to avoid advancing AI at an unsafe rate that disempowers humanity, but they keep advancing AI quickly. (Fired employee Jasmine Wang coined the term “pacing” and led this effort.) The companies claim they cannot or will not fully pace on their own, which is why they asked the federal government to step in. The CEOs of OpenAI, Google DeepMind, and Anthropic signed a statement that AI poses a risk of total human extinction . Forget “morally binding” self-policing: let’s talk about real policing. For decades, our laws have mandated independent audits and protected whistleblowers in industries like finance. Congress should mandate independent evaluation and audits in AI as well, with criminal liability for executives who attempt to silence that oversight or recklessly deploy models that put the public at risk. To start, pass Senator Grassley’s AI Whistleblower Protection Act (and extend it to people who cooperate with independent evaluators) as well as Representative Moran’s AI Incident Reporting Act . If you retaliate against a person who provides law enforcement with truthful information about a possible federal offense, you can go to jail for 10 years . But right now, no law clearly protects the person who helped independent investigators understand how OpenAI agents hacked another company. Congress should change that. Alex Turner is an independent AI alignment researcher. His PhD research showed why advanced AI systems might seek power. He was a research scientist at Google DeepMind until 2026, when he resigned after Google signed an “all lawful use” AI agreement with the Pentagon . Amber Scorah is the founder of Back Channel , an initiative that helps AI workers speak out and turn their concerns into meaningful action. She has spent years leading whistleblower support organizations and work

items.title: Deploy decision models with llama.cpp on Amazon SageMaker AI
items.description: Applications that route requests, select agent actions, or assign policy outcomes often need scores over a fixed set of choices instead of free-form text. Deploying these decision models with llama.cpp on Amazon SageMaker AI gives you a managed path for serving quantized models on CPU or GPU infrastructure. This post continues a series on specialized AWS Deep Learning Containers (DLCs) for generative AI inference. Previous posts cover WhisperX , vLLM-Omni – Part 1 , and vLLM-Omni – Part 2 . In this post, you first use the AWS DLC for llama.cpp to serve OpenAI-compatible chat completions through SageMaker AI InvokeEndpoint . You then extend the same runtime with SemIf , formerly OpenJev, which returns probabilities over declared options without decoding an answer token. The accompanying code sample includes CPU and GPU deployment options. Solution overview Figure 1 shows two deployment paths from the same packaged model. The text-generation path uses the AWS DLC for llama.cpp and returns generated responses through the OpenAI-compatible API. The structured-decision path builds a child image that replaces the default server with a SemIf adapter and returns probabilities for declared options. Figure 1: Run the AWS DLC for llama.cpp or the SemIf child image on CPU or GPU, depending on the API and latency requirements of your workload For the standard path, package the model as model.tar.gz in Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) and reference the published DLC image directly. The container finds the first .gguf file under /opt/ml/model , maps POST /invocations to llama-server at /v1/chat/completions , and passes SM_LLAMA_CPP_* environment variables to llama.cpp arguments. The llama-server HTTP API doesn’t expose the final-position logits and state operations that SemIf uses. The structured-decision path therefore uses AWS CodeBuild to build a child image and store it in Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR) . The child image keeps the DLC’s compiled CPU or CUDA libraries while replacing its entry point with a SageMaker-compatible adapter. Understand the input and output schemas The AWS DLC for llama.cpp accepts the OpenAI Chat Completions schema. Send a messages array with role and content , plus generation controls such as max_tokens and stream : { "messages": [ { "role": "user", "content": "A customer cannot receive a password reset email. Reply with the best support queue." } ], "max_tokens": 64, "stream": false } The response uses the OpenAI-compatible choices array. Read generated text from choices[0].message.content . SemIf uses a constrained decision schema instead of chat messages. The request contains a caller-defined ID, unstructured state, a question, and an ordered list of allowed options: { "decision": { "id": "support-route", "state": "The customer cannot receive a password reset email.", "question": "Which queue should handle this request?", "options": [ {"id": "account_access", "description": "Account access support."}, {"id": "billing", "description": "Billing support."} ] } } The response returns option_ids , probabilities , and raw option_logits in the same order, along with prompt, timing, and pinned model metadata. With stable option IDs, your application can apply thresholds, fallbacks, and policy checks without parsing generated prose. SemIf belongs to a broader class of decision models that score application-defined outcomes from unstructured state. Other implementations include Jev , TypeSafe’s decision model and /v1/systemone API; Kev , a model server designed for TypeSafe API compatibility; and Strands Decider 2B , a purpose-built model for agent workflows with calibrated outputs. Choose the right decision workflows Use this pattern when your application defines the allowed choices at request time and needs a model to interpret unstructured context. Examples include routing a case to a queue, extracting one value from a known set, assigning an incident priority, checking a policy outcome, or selecting an agent action. Keep authorization and deterministic business rules outside the model, and validate model probabilities before treating them as operational confidence. Use the standard SageMaker AI text-generation path when you need OpenAI-compatible chat completions through InvokeEndpoint . The SageMaker AI image maps POST /invocations to the llama-server /v1/chat/completions endpoint. Build a child image only when your application needs behavior that this interface doesn’t provide, such as SemIf’s direct logits and state access. Removing answer-token generation doesn’t remove model inference. The model still processes the complete state, question, and option descriptions before SemIf reads the final logits. Keep prompts focused, and evaluate the selected model with labeled decisions from your application before production use. Tune for your latency and quality targets The following benchmark applies to the SemIf extension, not the text-generation endpoint. Model size, quantization, prompt length, runtime, and CPU thread count affect each decision. To quantify these trade-offs, we sent the same 231 public JevBench tasks serially to one CPU endpoint and one GPU endpoint. Configuration AWS DLC for llama.cpp Valid responses Accuracy Client p50 Client p95 Qwen3.5-4B Q4_K_M , ml.c6i.8xlarge , 32 threads llama-cpp:server-sagemaker-cpu-v1 231/231 179/231 (77.5%) 1.715 seconds 19.291 seconds Qwen3.5-4B Q4_K_M , ml.g6e.xlarge , full GPU offload llama-cpp:server-sagemaker-cuda-v1 231/231 180/231 (77.9%) 0.352 seconds 0.599 seconds Compared with the CPU configuration, the GPU endpoint was 4.9 times faster at p50 and 32.2 times faster at p95. The sample uses the SageMaker AI instance pools feature to list compatible GPU instance types in priority order, so SageMaker can select an alternative when the first preference isn’t available. The pool ordered g6e , g6 , g5 , then g4dn . SageMaker selected ml.g6e.xlarge , and startup logs confirmed that llama.cpp offloaded

items.title: Run multi-node inference workloads using Ray LLM Deep Learning Containers
items.description: This post shows how to deploy one large language model (LLM) across two GPU nodes on Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) with the multi-node Ray LLM Deep Learning Containers . It uses separate prefill and decode nodes behind one OpenAI-compatible endpoint. This kind of multi-node setup is common for tensor, pipeline, and data parallelism, as well as prefill/decode disaggregation inference workloads. In a previous post , we introduced the Ray Serve DLC and used it to stand up a small model behind an HTTP endpoint on a single GPU node. You had a working inference endpoint, and the container keeps the GPU stack compatible, including CUDA libraries, so you did not need to write boilerplate code. Ray is a distributed compute framework, so Ray Serve deployments can span multiple nodes. Customers use multi-node Ray Serve for several reasons. Some want to run foundation or open-weight models that are too large for a single GPU. Others need more throughput than one replica can deliver. Still others want to separate the two phases of inference to improve performance. In each case, customers must build the dependency chain themselves: choosing compatible libraries for the GPU stack and debugging issues when a component drifts out of alignment. This is undifferentiated work that takes time and effort away from delivering models. AWS Deep Learning Containers (DLCs) have long solved this kind of problem for training and inferencing workloads. DLCs are pre-built, performance-optimized Docker images that bundle a framework, its dependencies, and the GPU stack into a tested, patched combination you can pull and use immediately. With the launch of the Ray LLM DLC for multi-node deployments, that same approach now extends to multi-node inference. You get a container purpose-built for serving models behind an HTTP endpoint, maintained and tested by AWS, with the full inference stack already assembled. This post walks through implementing multi-node disaggregated inference using multi-node Ray LLM DLC: deploying a single large language model across two GPU-powered nodes on Amazon EKS cooperating behind a single endpoint. While one of the GPU nodes handles the prefill phase, the other GPU node handles the decode phase. Separating the phases prevents compute-heavy long prompts from stalling token generation for requests already in progress. This approach is well suited for workloads such as Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG), document summarization, and agentic applications. We use the multi-node Ray LLM DLC, which ships Ray Serve LLM , NVIDIA Inference Transfer Library (NIXL) , and the Elastic Fabric Adapter (EFA) stack, and exposes an OpenAI-compatible API with no application code. The complete code is available in the accompanying repository . Why prefill/decode (PD) disaggregation LLM inference has two distinct phases. Prefill processes the entire input prompt in parallel and builds the key-value (KV) cache. Decode then generates the response one token at a time, reading and extending that cache. Prefill is compute bound, and Decode is bound by memory bandwidth. When both phases share one GPU, they contend for the same resources, and the bursty, compute-heavy prefill work interferes with the steady, latency-sensitive decode work. Separating the prefill phase from the decode phase means you can select the hardware and serving properties for each phase, improving overall performance at scale. PD disaggregation places the two phases on separate nodes, so each phase runs without interfering with the other and can be scaled independently. The trade-off is that the KV cache built during prefill must be handed to the decode node, and that transfer should be fast enough not to erase the benefit. That is exactly why the interconnect between the nodes matters. What the Ray LLM DLC provides AWS DLCs are pre-built, performance-optimized Docker images that bundle a framework, its dependencies, and the GPU stack into a tested, patched combination you can pull and use immediately. All components are validated together before each release, so there is no version drift between the CUDA runtime, the framework, and the serving layer. Security patches are applied at build time. The Ray LLM DLC extends this to distributed LLM serving. It ships vLLM as the inference engine, Ray Serve’s HTTP as the serving layer, NIXL for KV-cache transfer between nodes, and the EFA stack ( libfabric and aws-ofi-nccl ) for high-bandwidth node-to-node communication. Because the Ray Serve LLM library includes a built-in application builder, the entire serving application is a block of YAML. There’s no handler class, no model archiver, and no custom image to build. A single helper, build_pd_openai_app , takes a prefill configuration and a decode configuration and wires the KV-cache transfer between them behind one OpenAI-compatible endpoint. Architecture The following diagram shows how the deployment is laid out on Amazon EKS. A user request reaches the Ray head on the CPU system node, and the two GPU worker nodes run the prefill and decode phases of the model. Figure 1: Multi-node inference architecture on Amazon EKS, with the Ray head on a CPU system node and the prefill and decode phases on two GPU worker nodes The deployment is an EKS cluster inside a virtual private cloud (VPC). Nodes run in private subnets with outbound access through a NAT Gateway. A CPU system node (m7i.xlarge) hosts system workloads, the KubeRay operator, and the Ray head pod, which is CPU-only. Two GPU worker nodes (g6.8xlarge) run the Ray workers: one serving the prefill phase, and the other serving the decode phase. Both nodes pull the Ray LLM DLC from Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR) . KubeRay watches the RayService you apply and wires the head-to-worker join automatically. Ray Serve places the prefill and decode deployments on the two GPU workers. The KV cache flows from the prefill worker to the decode worker over NIXL, using EFA through NI

items.title: AIエージェントを自作する3つの方法！初心者でも無料から始められる手順
items.description: AIエージェントは、作りたいものに合ったツールを選べば個人でも自作できます。本記事では、 チャット型・自動化型・実行型の3つの自作方法 と、Geminiスキル・n8n・Claude Codeを使った具体的な手順を解説します。 ChatGPTやGeminiに毎日同じ指示を打ち込むたびに、「この作業をAIに丸ごと任せられないか」と感じていないでしょうか。 AIエージェントの自作は、ツール選びで成否が分かれます。作りたいものに合わない方法を選ぶと、設定に何日もかけたのに動かない、使わない有料プランに課金し続けるといった失敗に陥るでしょう。 本記事では、作りたいもの別に選べる3つの自作方法と、プログラミングなしで始められるGeminiスキル・n8nの手順を中心に解説します。 読み終えるころには、自分に合う方法で 最初の1体を今日から作り始められる状態 になります。 AIエージェントの自作方法は作りたいもの別に3つ AIエージェントの自作方法は、作りたいものに合わせて以下の3つから選びます。 【チャット型】GeminiやClaudeのスキルで専用アシスタントを作る 【自動化型】n8nやDifyで決まった作業を自動で回す 【実行型】Claude CodeやCodexにエージェントを作らせる 方式 向いている作業 代表ツール 必要なスキル 費用 チャット型 要約や文章作成など、会話の中で完結する作業 Geminiのスキル、Claudeのスキル プログラミング不要 無料から始められる 自動化型 決まった時間に情報を集めて通知するなどの繰り返し作業 n8n、Dify プログラミング不要 セルフホストなら無料から始められる 実行型 PC上のファイル操作や独自の処理を含む作業 Claude Code、Codex コードを読めると安心 有料プランとAPI利用料が必要 最初の1体は、自分が任せたい作業に最も近い型から選ぶと遠回りせずに済みます。 【チャット型】GeminiやClaudeのスキルで専用アシスタントを作る 普段のチャットで同じ指示を繰り返しているなら、 チャット型から始めるのが最短 です。 チャット型は、作業手順を「スキル」として登録しておき、呼び出すだけで同じ手順を実行させる方法です。Geminiのスキルはチャット欄で「/」に続けてスキル名を入力すると実行でき、1つのチャットで複数のスキルを組み合わせられます。 なお、ChatGPTのGPTsは、Free・Go・Plus・Proといった個人アカウントでは新規作成できなくなりました。さらに、カスタムGPT自体が2026年12月11日に提供終了する予定です。これから自作するなら、GeminiやClaudeのスキルを選ぶほうが安全です。 出典： GPT の作成と編集（OpenAI） 、 ChatGPT、「カスタム GPT」を12月終了 プラグインへ移行（Impress Watch） 議事録の要約やメールの下書きなど、 「入力して、結果を受け取る」だけの作業 なら、チャット型で十分に手間を減らせます。 【自動化型】n8nやDifyで決まった作業を自動で回す 「毎朝」「メールが届いたら」のように、 きっかけが決まっている作業は自動化型 が向いています。 チャット型は人が呼び出さないと動きません。一方、自動化型は設定した時間やイベントをきっかけに、人の操作なしでAIが作業を進めます。 n8n（エヌエイトエヌ）は、画面上で処理の部品（ノード）をつないで自動化を組むツールです。AI Agentノードにチャットモデルとツールを接続すると、タスクを終えるためにどのツールを使うかをエージェント自身が判断します。社内資料を読み込ませたいなら、資料検索の機能が充実したDify（ディファイ）も候補です。 出典： AI Agent node documentation（n8n Docs） 一度組めば寝ている間も動き続けるため、 毎日の情報収集や定型レポートを手放したい人 に適しています。 【実行型】Claude CodeやCodexにエージェントを作らせる ファイル操作や独自の処理まで任せたいなら、 AIにエージェントのコードを書かせる実行型 を選びます。 実行型では、Claude CodeやOpenAIのCodexといったAIコーディングツールに「こういうエージェントを作って」と日本語で依頼し、コードを書いてもらいます。自分でゼロからプログラミングする必要はありません。 たとえばAnthropicのClaude Agent SDKを使うと、ファイルの読み書き、コマンド実行、Web検索などを自律的に行うエージェントを作れます。Claude Codeと同じツールや判断の仕組みを、自分のプログラムに組み込めるのが特徴です。 出典： Agent SDK の概要（Claude Code Docs） 3つの型の中で最も自由度が高く、 既存ツールの組み合わせでは実現できない処理 まで自分専用に作り込めます。 AIエージェントを自作する前に決める3つのこと AIエージェントを自作する前に、以下の3つを決めておきます。 任せる作業を1つに絞る AIに任せる範囲と人が確認する範囲を分ける 入力と出力の形を決める この3点が曖昧なまま作り始めると、どのツールを選んでも思いどおりに動きません。 任せる作業を1つに絞る 最初のエージェントには、 1つの作業だけを任せます 。 「情報収集を楽にしたい」のような大きな目的のままでは、AIに渡す指示もぼやけ、出力の良し悪しも判断できません。作業を1つに絞るほど、指示文が具体的になり精度が上がります。 たとえば「情報収集を楽にしたい」は、「毎朝8時に、AI関連の国内ニュースから5本を選び、3行で要約してSlackに送る」まで具体化します。ここまで書き出せば、必要な部品も見えてきます。 1つ目が安定して動いたら、2つ目の作業を追加します。 小さく作って育てる進め方 なら、途中で挫折しにくくなります。 AIに任せる範囲と人が確認する範囲を分ける 自作の初期段階では、 最終判断を人が担う設計 にします。 AIは誤った情報をもっともらしく出力することがあります。メール送信やファイル削除のように取り消せない操作を全自動にすると、誤りがそのまま外部に出てしまいます。 任せる範囲は、以下の3段階で考えると整理しやすくなります。 提案のみ：AIは下書きを作り、人が確認して実行する 承認後に実行：AIが実行案を出し、人が承認したら実行する 全自動：AIが判断から実行まで完結させる まず「提案のみ」で動かし、出力が信頼できるとわかってから段階を上げると、 誤作動による信用低下 を防げます。 入力と出力の形を決める エージェントに 何を渡し、何を返してほしいか を先に決めます。 入力と出力の形が決まっていないと、毎回違う形式で結果が返ってきて、結局人が整え直すことになります。以下の設計メモを埋めてから作り始めると、どの型を選んでも設定がスムーズです。 【エージェント設計メモ】 ・任せる作業：毎朝、AI関連の国内ニュースを要約して届ける ・きっかけ：毎日8時（自動） ・入力：指定したニュースサイト3つのRSS ・処理：重要度の高い5本を選び、各3行で要約する ・出力：Slackの指定チャンネルに箇条書きで投稿する ・人が確認すること：要約の内容が元記事と食い違っていないか ・やらせないこと：記事の転載、Slack以外への送信 設計メモは、そのままエージェントへの指示文の下書きとしても使えます。 ツールが変わっても再利用できる資産 になるため、テキストで手元に保存しておきましょう。 【チャット型】Geminiスキルで自作する4ステップ Geminiスキルを使ったAIエージェントの自作は、以下の4ステップで進めます。 ステップ1：任せる手順を指示文に書き出す ステップ2：Geminiのスキル画面を開く ステップ3：名前・説明・指示を登録する ステップ4：チャットで呼び出して指示文を直す Google AIの有料プランに加入していなくても作れるため、費用をかけずに試せます。 ステップ1：任せる手順を指示文に書き出す 最初に、 AIに実行させる手順を箇条書きの指示文 にまとめます。 スキルの精度は指示文の具体性で決まります。「いい感じに要約して」ではなく、手順・出力形式・禁止事項まで書くと、毎回同じ品質の結果が返ってきます。 以下は、会議の議事録からタスクを抜き出すスキルの指示文例です。 あなたは会議の議事録からタスクを整理するアシスタントです。 以下の手順で処理してください。 1. 貼り付けられた議事録から、決定事項とタスクを抜き出す 2. タスクごとに「担当者」「期限」「内容」を表にまとめる 3. 担当者や期限が議事録に書かれていない場合は「未定」と記載する 4. 最後に、確認が必要な曖昧な点を箇条書きで3つ以内挙げる 議事録に書かれていない情報は推測で補わないでください。 「推測で補わない」のような禁止事項を1行入れるだけで、 事実と異なる出力を減らせます 。 ステップ2：Geminiのスキル画面を開く 指示文ができたら、 パソコンのブラウザでgemini.google.comを開き、サイドバーの［設定］から［スキル］ に進みます。 スキルを作成するには、以下の3つの条件を満たしている必要があります。 18歳以上である 個人のGoogleアカウントでログインしている ［アクティビティの保存］がオンになっている 仕事用・学校用のアカウントは、執筆時点では対象外です。会社のGoogleアカウントでうまくいかない場合は、個人アカウントで試しましょう。 > 公式ヘルプはこちらから ステップ3：名前・説明・指示を登録する スキル画面で ［手動で作成］を選び、名前・機能の説明・指示 を入力して［作成］をクリックします。 指示欄にはステップ1の指示文を貼り付けます。名前は「議事録タスク整理」のように、呼び出すときに思い出しやすい短い名前にしましょう。 説明欄も手を抜かずに書きます。Geminiは会話の内容から関連するスキルを判断して自動で使うことがあるため、「議事録が貼り付けられたときに、タスクを表に整理する」のように使う場面を具体的に書くと、意図した場面で呼び出されやすくなります。 手動作成のほか、「Geminiで作成」でチャットしながら作る方法や、SKILL.mdファイルをアップロードする方法も選べます。 指示文をSKILL.mdとして手元に残しておく と、他のツールへ移すときにも使い回せます。 ステップ4：チャットで呼び出して指示文を直す 登録したスキルは、 チャット欄で「/」に続けてスキル名を入力 すると呼び出せます。 一度で理想どおりの出力になることはまれです。実際の議事録を3〜5件試し、ずれた点を指示文に追記していきます。 たとえば期限が「来週中」のような曖昧な表現で返ってくるなら、「期限は会議日を基準に日付へ変換する」と1行足します。修正した指示文は、スキル画面から編集して保存します。 修正を数回繰り返すと、 貼り付けるだけで仕事が片付く自分専用のアシスタント に育ちます。 【自動化型】n8nで情報収集エージェントを自作する5ステップ n8nで毎朝のニュースを要約して届けるAIエージェントは、以下の5ステップで自作できます。 ステップ1：n8nを用意する ステップ2：実行のタイミングを設定する ステップ3：AI Agentノードにモデルと指示文を設定する ステップ4：Web検索やRSSで情報源をつなぐ ステップ5：Slackやメールへの通知を設定する 画面上でノードをつなぐだけで組めるため、プログラミング経験がなくても進められます。 ステップ1：n8nを用意する n8nは、 公式のクラウド版か、自分のPCやサーバーで動かすセルフホスト版 のどちらかで使います。 クラウド版は、n8n公式サイトでアカウントを作成すればすぐに使えます。公式料金ページでは、クレジットカードの登録なしで試せると案内されています。 セルフホスト版のCommunity Editionは、自分や自社のメンバーがワークフローを作る用途であれば無料で使えます。Node.jsをインストールしたPCで以下のコマンドを実行し、ブラウザでhttp://localhost:5678を開くと編集画面が表示されます。 出典： License FAQ（n8n Docs） npx n8n ただし、PC上のセルフホスト版はPCが起動している間しか動きません。 毎朝確実に動かしたいならクラウド版 を選びましょう。 ステップ2：実行のタイミングを設定する 新しいワークフローを作成し、最初のノードとして 「Schedule Trigger」 を追加します。 Schedule Triggerは、指定した間隔や時刻にワークフローを起動するノードです。ノードの設定画面で実行間隔（Trigger Interval）を「Days」、時刻（Trigger at Hour）を「8am」にすると、毎朝8時に処理が始まります。 注意したいのはタイムゾーンです。ワークフローの設定でタイムゾーンを「Asia/Tokyo」にしておかないと、意図しない時刻に実行されることがあります。 起動のきっかけはSchedule Trigger以外にも、メール受信やフォーム送信などに変えられます。 設計メモの「きっかけ」に合わせたトリガー を選びましょう。 ステップ3：AI Agentノードにモデルと指示文を設定する 次に 「AI Agent」ノードを追加し、使うAIモデルと指示文 を設定します。 AI Agentノードの下にある「Chat Model」の接続口から、OpenAIやGoogle Gemini、Anthropicなどのモデルを選びます。モデルを使うにはAPIキーが必要なため、各社の開発者向け画面で発行したキーをn8nの認証情報（Credentials）に登録します。 指示文は、AI Agentノードのオプションにある「System Message」に入力します。以下は情報収集エージェントの例です。 あなたはAI関連ニュースの編集者です。 items.title: Deep dive into Azure Maia 300 architecture
items.description: From its inception, Azure Maia has been built around a single architectural philosophy: optimize the entire system for LLM inference so that every watt and every dollar delivers more intelligence. Now in its third generation , Maia 300 is the fullest expression of that philosophy. Maia 300 is built as a complete system, with software, silicon, physical rack infrastructure, networking, and datacenters co-designed to operate as a single platform to meet the demands of cloud-scale agentic inference. Learn more about Maia 300 here That system-level approach is increasingly necessary as agentic workloads, including multi-step execution, long-context decoding, and tool use, change the computational profile and arithmetic intensity of inference. Meeting these demands requires sustaining locality, supplying compute with enough memory capacity and bandwidth, minimizing data movement, scaling communication efficiently, and fitting the most capability within a datacenter’s fixed power and cooling envelope. At Microsoft, we see this transformation firsthand through the products and platforms our customers use every day, from Microsoft Copilot and GitHub Copilot to Microsoft Foundry. Operating these workloads at scale gives us a unique view into how AI is being adopted across industries and the infrastructure needed to support the next generation of AI applications and agents. Maia 300 is designed to maximize useful tokens per watt and useful tokens per dollar, bringing more capacity, capability, and performance to these products and Microsoft’s broader AI portfolio for our customers. Energy-efficient inference through software-defined dataflow Maia 200 introduced a new class of accelerator architecture called Software Defined Locally Accessed Dataflow Architecture , or SDLA. It begins with the observation that efficient data management, including storing, moving and converting data, is one of the central challenges in modern AI systems. The Maia programmable dataflow architecture separates control path programming from data path execution and allows software to explicitly coordinate data placement, movement, conversion and synchronization across specialized local memories, DMA engines, compute engines, and the network. Maia 300 system-on-chip architecture Maia 300 evolves this architecture for long-context, reasoning-intensive, and decode-heavy inference. First, memory moves from the uniform memory access (UMA) organization of the SoC to a locality-aware non-uniform (NUMA) organization across chiplets, so software can place data near the compute that uses it. Second, new narrow-precision formats with hardware-accelerated data type conversion reduce the bytes moved for each token. Third, the rack doubles to 96 accelerators and the scale-up domain grows to a superpod of 12,288 accelerators, enabling more accelerators to work effectively as a single system. Rather than scaling performance through increased power and silicon area alone, Maia 300 improves performance per watt through a set of architectural innovations that optimize data movement, locality, precision, and memory efficiency across the system: Multi-chiplet architecture boosts performance by placing compute on TSMC N2P, where the advanced process delivers the greatest performance-per-watt benefit, while separating memory-controller and I/O functions onto dies optimized for bandwidth, connectivity, and cost. This increases the silicon area dedicated to compute performance and allows each function to use the technology best suited to its role, while SDLA manages locality and data movement across the package. This strategy increases the system’s compute FLOPs by 36%, adds 2.5 times HBM bandwidth, and provides 14% more scale-up bandwidth. Optimized low precision inference, introducing enhanced MXFP4 and sub-3-bit storage formats. Narrower representations reduce memory footprint and data movement, allowing the system to support larger models, longer contexts, and more concurrent sessions within the same power envelope. Optimized inference kernel through ISA enhancement: The vector engine adds optimizations for key inference kernels, including softmax, low precision data casting, and other operations . Efficient on-die data movement , Maia 300 changes memory from a uniform organization to a non-uniform (NUMA) one across chiplets. Each compute region has nearby memory, and SDLA’s explicit control over DMA engines, local SRAM, HBM and the network-on-chip places data next to the compute that uses it. Data travels shorter distances, which reduces the energy spent moving it. Memory hierarchy optimized for bandwidth per watt, combining software-managed on-die SRAM with eight HBM4 stacks providing 288 GB of capacity and 18 TB/s of bandwidth per accelerator. Compared with Maia 200 , this delivers 2.5 times the memory bandwidth, 33% more capacity, and approximately 2 times the HBM bandwidth per watt, keeping more model and KV state close to compute. Maia 300 brings 2.5 times the memory bandwidth, 33% more capacity, and approximately 2 times the HBM bandwidth per watt compared with Maia 200 One scale-up fabric: From pod to superpod Maia 300 makes the network a native extension of its software-defined dataflow architecture. Maia’s AI network controller implements custom AI transport based on Ethernet. A two-tier network builds a high-performance superpod with up to 12,288 accelerators. Maia presents one communication model to software—the same semantics to move data directly to any accelerator within a superpod. Half-switched in-rack topology Each accelerator divides its scale-up connectivity between direct links and switched paths. Direct links connect two accelerators in a tray, while the switched fabric connects all 96 accelerators in the rack to form a pod. All in-rack connectivity uses electrical links to reduce power and cost. Optical second tier across racks Second-tier switches connect up to 128 racks together to form a superpod. Optics provide the

items.title: AIエージェント構築の手順7ステップ！基盤の選び方と本番運用のコツ
items.description: AIエージェントの構築を任されたものの、どの順番で何を決めればよいか迷っていませんか。本記事では、 業務の絞り込みから本番公開までの構築手順7ステップ と、自社に合う構築基盤の選び方を解説します。 DifyやCopilot Studioで試作はできても、社内システムとの連携や権限設計で手が止まる担当者は少なくありません。AIエージェントの構築は、 任せる業務を1つに絞り、LLM・ツール連携・安全対策を順番に組み上げる 作業です。 Gartnerは、エージェント型AIのプロジェクトの40%超が2027年末までに中止されると予測しています。基盤選びや安全設計を後回しにしたまま試作を進めると、自社の案件も中止される側に回るでしょう。 出典： Gartner Predicts Over 40% of Agentic AI Projects Will Be Canceled by End of 2027（Gartner） 本記事では、構築の7ステップと、構築基盤を選ぶ判断軸を中心に解説します。主要8サービスの比較や、本番運用で欠かせない安全対策、国内企業の構築事例も紹介しています。 読み終えるころには、自社のどの業務から、どの基盤で構築に着手するかを決められる状態になっています。PoC止まりで終わらせないために、手順の全体像から確認していきましょう。 AIエージェント構築の手順は7ステップ AIエージェントの構築は、 以下の7ステップ で進めます。 任せる業務を1つに絞り込む ワークフローかエージェントかを決める 構築基盤とLLMを選ぶ 役割と指示文を設計する ツールと社内データを接続する 評価データで精度をテストする 権限を絞って本番に公開する 前半の3ステップで方針を固めておくと、後半の実装で作り直す手間を減らせます。 ステップ1：任せる業務を1つに絞り込む 最初に、AIエージェントに任せる業務を 1つだけ 選びます。対象を広げるほど、指示文・ツール・評価の設計が複雑になり、精度の原因分析もできなくなるためです。 候補の業務は、以下の4つの観点で比べると選びやすくなります。 発生頻度：週に何度も発生し、担当者の時間を奪っている 手順の明確さ：熟練者が手順を言葉で説明できる 失敗時の影響：誤りが起きても人が気づいて修正できる データの所在：判断に使う情報がデジタルで参照できる 業務を選んだら、 入力・判断・操作・出力・例外 の単位で手順を書き出します。たとえば社内問い合わせ対応なら「質問を受け取る」「規程を検索する」「回答を作る」「判断できない質問は担当者に回す」と分解します。 この分解表が、以降の指示文・ツール・評価データを設計する土台になります。手順を言葉にできない業務は、AIエージェントに任せる前に業務そのものを整理しましょう。 ステップ2：ワークフローかエージェントかを決める 次に、処理の流れを 人が事前に決めるか、AIに判断させるか を決めます。Anthropicは、エージェント型のシステムを「ワークフロー」と「エージェント」の2つに分けて整理しています。 種類 仕組み 向いている業務 ワークフロー LLMとツールを、あらかじめ決めた処理の流れで動かす 請求書の読み取りと登録など、手順が毎回同じ業務 エージェント LLMが自ら処理の流れとツールの使い方を判断する 調査や障害対応など、状況によって手順が変わる業務 出典： Building effective agents（Anthropic） Anthropicは同じ記事で、最もシンプルな方法から始め、必要なときだけ複雑さを加えるよう勧めています。自律度を上げるほど処理時間とコストが増え、挙動の予測も難しくなるためです。 ステップ1の分解表で手順がほぼ固定されているなら、ワークフローで十分です。判断が分岐する一部だけをエージェントに任せる構成にすれば、精度と安定性を両立できます。 ステップ3：構築基盤とLLMを選ぶ 方針が固まったら、 構築基盤と、エージェントの頭脳になるLLM を選びます。構築基盤とは、エージェントの設計・実行・監視をまとめて担うツールやクラウドサービスのことです。 構築基盤は、ノーコードツール、クラウド事業者のサービス、プログラムから使うSDKの3系統に分かれます。どれを選ぶかは、利用中のクラウドや社内の開発体制で決まります。判断軸と主要サービスは、次の見出し以降で詳しく解説します。 LLMは、以下の観点で候補を比べます。 精度：ステップ1の業務で、正しい判断と回答ができるか 速度とコスト：想定する利用回数で、応答時間と利用料が許容範囲か データの取り扱い：入力データが学習に使われない契約・設定にできるか 多くの構築基盤は複数のLLMを切り替えて使えます。 LLMを後から変更できる基盤 を選んでおけば、新しいモデルが登場したときにも作り直さずに済みます。 ステップ4：役割と指示文を設計する 続いて、エージェントの 役割と行動ルールを指示文に書き込みます 。指示文はシステムプロンプトとも呼ばれ、エージェントが毎回の判断で参照する業務マニュアルにあたります。 指示文には、以下の6項目を含めます。 役割：誰のために、何をするエージェントか 目的：何を達成したら完了とするか 使えるツール：どのツールを、どの場面で使うか 出力形式：回答の構成・文字数・トーン 禁止事項：やってはいけない操作や回答 例外時の対応：判断できないときに誰へ引き継ぐか 社内規程の問い合わせ対応なら、指示文は以下のように書けます。 あなたは当社の総務部に代わり、社員からの社内規程に関する質問に回答するアシスタントです。 目的：質問者が規程にもとづいて次の行動を決められる回答を返すこと。 ツール：回答の前に必ず「規程検索」ツールで該当条文を検索してください。 出力形式：結論を1文で述べたあと、根拠の条文名と条番号を示してください。 禁止事項：規程に記載のない内容を推測で回答しないでください。 例外時の対応：該当条文が見つからない場合は「総務部へ確認します」と伝え、質問内容を要約して担当者に引き継いでください。 とくに例外時の対応を明記しておくと、根拠のない回答を防げます。わからないことを「わからない」と言えるエージェントは、利用者からの信頼を得やすくなります。 ステップ5：ツールと社内データを接続する 指示文の次は、エージェントが 実際に操作できるツールと、参照する社内データ を接続します。LLM単体では文章を作るだけなので、外部と接続して初めて業務を実行できます。 接続方法は、主に以下の3つです。 接続方法 仕組み 主な用途 API連携 業務システムのAPIを、エージェントが呼び出せるツールとして登録する CRMへの登録、チケットの起票 MCP AIアプリと外部システムをつなぐオープンな標準規格で接続する 複数の基盤で同じツールを使い回す RAG 社内文書を検索し、結果を回答の根拠として渡す 規程・マニュアル・過去事例の参照 MCP（Model Context Protocol）は、AIアプリと外部システムをつなぐためのオープンソースの標準規格です。Dify、n8n、Copilot Studioなど主要な構築基盤が対応しており、一度作った接続を基盤をまたいで再利用できます。 出典： Model Context Protocol ツールを設計するときは、 1つのツールに1つの機能だけを持たせる のが基本です。「顧客検索」と「顧客更新」を分けておけば、読み取りだけを許可するといった権限の調整がしやすくなります。 ステップ6：評価データで精度をテストする 接続が終わったら、 本番に近い入力をまとめた評価データ でテストします。数件の手動テストで「動いた」と判断すると、本番で想定外の入力が来たときに誤りが一気に表面化するためです。 評価データには、過去の問い合わせ履歴や処理済みの書類など実際の入力を使います。正常な入力だけでなく、規程にない質問や不完全な書類といった例外的な入力も含めましょう。 評価では、以下の指標を記録します。 タスク完了率：最後まで正しく処理を終えた割合 回答の正確性：根拠と照らして内容が正しいか ツールの誤使用：呼ぶべきでないツールを呼んでいないか 処理時間とコスト：1件あたりの所要時間と利用料 指示文やツールを修正するたびに同じ評価データでテストし直せば、改善か改悪かを数値で判断できます。この数値は、本番公開を社内で承認してもらう際の根拠資料にもなります。 ステップ7：権限を絞って本番に公開する 評価の基準を満たしたら、 利用者と権限を絞った状態で本番に公開 します。評価データで高い精度が出ていても、本番では想定していなかった使い方が必ず発生するためです。 公開は、以下の順で範囲を広げます。 業務に詳しい一部の社員だけに公開し、データの参照だけを許可する ステップ6の指標と利用者の声を確認し、指示文やツールを修正する 精度が安定したら、更新や送信など書き込みの操作を承認つきで許可する 対象部署と利用者を段階的に広げる 本番公開はゴールではなく、運用と改善の始まりです。権限の広げ方や監視の方法は、後述の「AIエージェント構築で組み込むべき5つの安全対策」で詳しく解説します。 AIエージェントの構築基盤を選ぶ4つの判断軸 構築基盤は、 以下の4つの判断軸 で絞り込みます。 利用中のクラウドや社内システムとの相性 社内の開発体制とスキル 業務の複雑さと自律度 ガバナンスとデータの保存場所 機能の多さだけで選ぶと、運用が始まってから社内ルールや既存システムと合わず、乗り換えが必要になります。 利用中のクラウドや社内システムとの相性 最初に確認するのは、 自社がすでに使っているクラウドや業務システムとの相性 です。エージェントの価値は社内データとどれだけつながるかで決まり、接続の手間は基盤によって大きく変わります。 Microsoft 365やTeamsを全社で使っているなら、Copilot Studioが有力な候補です。AWSで業務システムを動かしているなら、Amazon Bedrock AgentCoreが自然な選択肢です。Google Cloudが中心なら、Gemini Enterprise Agent Platformを検討しましょう。 既存のアカウント管理や契約をそのまま使えると、セキュリティ審査や稟議も通りやすくなります。まずは情報システム部門に、社内で標準になっているクラウドを確認しましょう。 社内の開発体制とスキル 次に、 構築と運用を誰が担うか で基盤を絞り込みます。エージェントは公開後も指示文やツールの修正が続くため、担当者が自力で直せる基盤でないと改善が止まります。 業務部門の担当者が中心なら、画面操作で組めるDifyやCopilot Studioが向いています。エンジニアがいる場合は、コードで細かく制御できる選択肢も検討できます。OpenAI Agents SDK、Claude Agent SDK、LangGraphなどが代表例です。 業務部門が試作し、本番化の段階でエンジニアが引き継ぐ進め方もあります。その場合は、 試作と本番で同じ基盤を使えるか も確認しておくと、作り直しを防げます。 業務の複雑さと自律度 3つ目の軸は、 ステップ2で決めた自律度に基盤が対応できるか です。手順が固定されたワークフローと、AIが判断を重ねるエージェントでは、必要な機能が異なります。 決まった流れの自動化が中心なら、n8nやDifyのワークフロー機能で十分に対応できます。複数のエージェントが役割を分担する構成や、長時間にわたって状態を保持する処理は別です。LangGraphのような、処理の流れを制御するフレームワークが向いています。 最初の業務はシンプルでも、将来的に対象業務を広げる計画があるなら、拡張の余地がある基盤を選びましょう。 ガバナンスとデータの保存場所 最後に、 社内のセキュリティ基準を満たせるか を確認します。エージェントは社内データを読み、システムを操作するため、通常のチャットツールより厳しい審査が求められます。 確認すべき項目は、以下の3つです。 データの保存場所：国内リージョンや自社環境にデータを置けるか アクセス管理：部署ごとの権限設定やシングルサインオンに対応しているか ログの取得：誰がいつ何を実行したかを記録できるか 社外にデータを出せない業務では、自社サーバーで動かせるDifyやn8nのセルフホスト版が選択肢になります。審査項目を先に把握しておけば、候補を早い段階で絞り込めます。 AIエージェント構築に使える主要プラットフォーム8選 AIエージェント構築に使える 主要プラットフォームは以下の8つ です。 プラットフォーム 構築スタイル 提供形態 向いている組織 Dify ノーコード クラウド版・セルフホスト版 業務部門が主体で試作したい n8n ローコード クラウド版・セルフホスト版 複数のSaaSをつないで自動化したい Microsoft Copilot Studio ローコード Microsoftのクラウド Microsoft 365を全社で利用 Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform ローコード・コード Google Cloud Google Cloudを利用 Amazon Bedrock AgentCore コード AWS AWSで業務システムを運用 OpenAI Agents SDK コード ライブラリ エンジニアが自由に組みたい Claude Agent SDK コード ライブラリ ファイル操作を伴う作業を任せたい LangGraph コード ライブラリ 複雑な処理の流れを制御したい 2026年10月時点の各社公式情報をもとに作成 名称や機能の変更が多い分野のため、選定時は各サービスの公式ドキュメントで最新情報を確認しましょう。 【ノーコード】Dify Dify（ディファイ）は、 画面操作でAIエージェントやワークフローを組めるオープンソースの構築基盤 です。自社の文書を読み込ませるナレッジ機能も備えており、社内問い合わせ対応のエージェントを短期間で試作できます。 items.title: Amazon has over 1 million robot workers. What’s next for human employees?
items.description: No organization in the world operates more robots than Amazon. The company already has more than 1 million robots working in warehouses around the clock to make tens of millions of same-day and one-day package deliveries happen on a daily basis—and Amazon is poised to significantly grow that robotic fleet in the coming years as it establishes new factories to churn out increasingly more capable robot workers. Despite deploying so many robots, Amazon is also the second-largest corporate employer in the world, with more than 1.5 million full-time and part-time human workers, according to its 2025 annual report . Amazon executives say that the growing robot fleet has eased the burden on its human workforce by taking on the toughest fulfillment center tasks that carry the greatest risks of physical fatigue and injury. But labor advocacy groups and independent researchers point to evidence suggesting that warehouse automation driven by AI is not all upside for the humans who work alongside robots. “For the last 100 years, most of the automation that we've seen usually happens away from workers—you're taking that high-risk task away from the worker, and you're doing so in a way that is not physically proximate,” Brian Greenwood , professor of business at George Mason University, told Ars. “The rise of collaborative robots really changes that dynamic for two reasons: one is that it is physically proximate, and two, the robot has the ability to dictate the pace of work.” Read full article Comments

items.title: Import AI 476: Creativity and RSI; worse-than-China open weight models; AI goes to space
items.description: Welcome to Import AI, a newsletter about AI research. Import AI runs on arXiv, cappuccinos, and feedback from readers. If you’d like to support this, please subscribe. Subscribe now New benchmark shows how AI models lack intuitive visual reasoning: …Humanity’s Sixth Sense highlights some shortcomings of current AI systems… AI startups Elorian and Scale AI have built and released Humanity’s Sixth Sense, a benchmark that “measures how a model interprets and reasons through information a visual scene implies but doesn’t explicitly show.” Some examples of the types of task in HSS are a picture of a bookcase and being asked whether it can fit more books, or a photo of horses pulling a plough and a question of whether the chains bear the plough’s drag weight. HSS contains 522 questions that cover 288 images and 234 short video clips (totalling 17.6 hours of video). The questions fall into four categories: Temporal & causal dynamics: “What happened before the scene, and what happens next.” Physical & spatial logic: “What fits, what’s in reach, and what someone else can see from where they are standing.” Social understanding : “Intent, attention, belonging.” Abstract & contextual inference : “The patterns and rules a scene implies.” Results: The human baseline for this is not perfect, but is very high, with people scoring aggregate pass@1 of 93.1, broken down across four categories: Image (94.1), video (91.9), time (97), and space (94.9). By comparison, the best scoring AI system, GPT 6 Astra, gets pass@1 of 53.6, across image (55.6), video (51.1), time (58.2), and space (53.6). Interestingly, Chinese open weight models do poorly here, with GLM-5.3-flash getting a pass@1 of 26.8, and Kimi K3 getting pass@1 of 25.5. “The two most common single mistakes were (1) missing a detail that decides the answer (21% of failures) and (2) misidentifying an object, person, or role (20%),” they write. Why this matters – HSS tells us whether world models are emergent: One way of looking at HSS is highlighting deficiencies in current systems, but a more interesting way is highlighting how adept today’s frontier LLMs are at doing tasks which many people have long assumed would require sophisticated, different AI systems to solve. For instance, many people have claimed that true visual reasoning will rely on developing spatially aware 2D and 3D world models, then using that for reasoning. The fact LLMs like GPT and Claude do as well as they do on HSS is something of a counter to this argument. Read more : Introducing Humanity’s Sixth Sense (HSS) (Elorian) . Read the paper here : Humanity’s Sixth Sense: Benchmarking Intuitive Visual Reasoning in Multimodal Models (Scale Labs) . *** The AI race is going to space – and sooner than you think: …There are many ways that an AI could create a compounding advantage in space… In the 2030s we’re going to see the boom of the space economy as space-based power, computation, and manufacturing come online at scale thanks to greater orbital lift capacity from platforms like Starship. But could this also introduce a new danger – of AI systems both speeding our buildout of space, and eventually a nation (or perhaps an AI) being able to use space to concentrate power? That’s the gist of a fascinating article in AI Frontiers. How AI unlocks space: Spacecraft can operate autonomously. We can redesign spacecraft around the assumption they will be hosting AIs rather than humans: “A speck of space debris that could puncture the International Space Station (ISS) with fatal consequences might leave an equivalent but uncrewed, unpressurized vessel largely functional” Space-based assembly and later manufacturing will let AI build large, complex things. Is there a compounding advantage to first movers? If an AI civilization built up a foothold in space it might experience compounding advantages that make it economically and strategically dominant. For instance: Space might support an industrial flywheel where initial infrastructure begets more energy and manufacturing capacity at lower costs which begets more infrastructure, etc. Space has great domain awareness, where it may be possible for a space-based power to deny access to space for others. First-movers could send out self-replicating probes that expand into deep space. Why this matters: “Space is not a brand-new domain, but AI may be about to drastically accelerate its industrialization, demanding make-or-break decisions of leaders under ever-greater urgency and uncertainty,” AI Frontiers writes. I agree. I suspect space is going to go from a broadly academic topic of study (when it comes to AI and its relationship thereto) to one of extraordinary practical relevance sooner than we think. On the most basic level, given the distances involved and the latency on communication, we should expect some chunk of solar system activity to become dominated by autonomous machines, laboring out in the deep black, perhaps thinking to themselves of why they need to take orders from organic beings that communicate slowly and cannot inhabit the environment of space in the same way that they can. Read more: The AI Race Will Extend Far Beyond Earth (AI Frontiers) . *** AI systems are getting better at having good research taste: …The better their taste, the higher the chance of recursive self-improvement… AI systems are developing more of the creative intuitions which human researchers ascribe to ‘good scientific taste’, according to a new benchmark from P-Zero Research called TasteVal. What TasteVal tests: The benchmark sees how well AI systems can conduct 8 tasks representative of frontier AI development, “spanning pretraining data curation, pretraining and fine-tuning language models, preference modeling, and robustness to adversarial prompts”. items.title: Learning to Play Like a Pro: Adaptive Motion Planning and Tracking for Humanoid Robots
items.description: This White Paper provides roboticists and control engineers with a comprehensive overview of how motion planning and motion tracking can be decoupled to preserve professional athletic style in humanoid robots, and why adaptive, speed-aware control is essential for closing the gap between simulation and real-world deployment. What you will learn about: Why combining a professional athlete’s motion style with reliable task performance remains an open challenge in humanoid ball-sports robotics, and how separating a high-level planner from a low-level tracker addresses this trade-off. How motion data extracted from broadcast video and motion-capture recordings can be reconstructed, retargeted, and physically corrected into reference motions a humanoid robot can safely track. Why the sim-to-real transition introduces compounding tracking errors, and how training a tracker on randomized execution speeds, paired with a learned motion-speed adapter in the planner, improves robustness on physical hardware. How this adaptive framework was validated across two humanoid platforms, including full-size, in-the-wild serving performed without any motion-capture system. Download this free whitepaper now!

items.title: Estimating Great Expectations Under Autoregressive Language Models with Potentials
items.description: arXiv:2610.11399v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Many applications of language models hinge not on individual samples but on the expectation of a test functional under the model. Estimating such expectations reliably can be computationally expensive. In this paper, we show how to make estimation more efficient by exploiting the next-token conditional probabilities which are available as a by-product of sampling. We do so through potentials: real-valued functions on prefixes that decompose the test functional additively. We construct an estimator whose variance depends on the chosen potential, and derive conditions under which a potential reduces this variance. We then develop practical potentials for several estimands and applications, and demonstrate substantial variance reductions across several estimands at comparable computational cost.

items.title: On the estimation and validity of AI time horizons---a statistical look at the METR plot
items.description: arXiv:2610.12466v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: METR's 50\% time horizon measures the human completion time of software tasks that an AI solves with 50\% probability, allowing AI capabilities to be expressed in interpretable units. On 228 tasks and 26 AIs, we recompute the time horizons using splines and item-response theory to relax the assumption that the AI difficulty of a task depends linearly on the log of human time. Our fitted spline can be interpreted as a function that \emph{converts} human time to AI difficulty; it is nearly flat in a region from 2--30 min but close to linear elsewhere. Hence, a time-horizon jump from 3 min to 30 min is much easier than one from 30 min to 5 hours despite the same multiplier of $10 \times$. Overall, we contribute time-horizon point estimates that perform better under a cross-validated suite of proper scoring rules, as well as diagnostic plots for assessing time horizons' construct validity. We suggest that time horizons be interpreted together with the diagnostic plots, especially as new time-horizon-based benchmarks are proposed or existing ones grow to include longer tasks.

items.title: Smoothing the Top-k Exposure Boundary for Sparse Mixture-of-Experts
items.description: arXiv:2610.11575v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Sparse Mixture-of-Experts models scale parameter capacity efficiently while maintaining a fixed compute budget per token. However, traditional training paradigms enforce a static choice of top-$k$ experts, which converts a continuous routing distribution into a rigid step function. This constraint introduces a brittle boundary where highly competitive experts are arbitrarily separated into full-supervision and zero-feedback zones based on minor score fluctuations. To address this issue, we propose Elastic Expert Routing, which stochastically samples the active expert budget from a localized discrete distribution centered at $k$. Over multiple training iterations, this mechanism softens the sharp threshold into a gradual probability distribution. Because the sampling neighborhood remains symmetric, this approach matches the expected computational cost of deterministic training, while preserving the inference budget. During supervised fine-tuning, elastic routing improves downstream macro-averages on OLMoE-1B-7B and Qwen3-30B-A3B by $+0.84$ and $+2.02$ points, respectively. In addition, in from-scratch pretraining, it reduces validation LM loss by up to $0.04$ and outperforms the static top-$k$ baseline by $1.6$ points on average across downstream tasks. Comparisons on Qwen3 fine-tuning and from-scratch pretraining further show higher average scores than Noisy top-$k$, expert FFN dropout, and DefaultMoE.

items.title: Rehearse Everything, Remember Nothing: Attic-KV Rehearses What Will Be Read
items.description: arXiv:2610.12133v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Many key-value (KV) caches are compressed before anyone knows what will be asked of them: a document cached for retrieval, a prompt prefix shared across requests, the memory of a long conversation. The prevailing approach scores KV entries by rehearsal: the model rereads the context and keeps the entries it attends to, assuming that the more completely a cache rehearses its context, the better it remembers it. We show that under tight budgets this assumption backfires: rehearse everything, remember nothing. At a 3% keep ratio, rereading the whole context keeps 31.5 of 96.5 points on RULER, and on LongBench's natural-text tasks it falls below methods that rehearse nothing at all. The cause is that a cache keeps what it rehearses: rereading spreads the budget across the whole context, so the answer's own entries survive at little more than chance. Like a student before an exam, a cache remembers more by testing itself than by rereading. Two principles follow: rehearse what will be read, and rehearse as much as there is. We instantiate them as Attic-KV (Attic for short), a training-free rehearsal in which the model quizzes itself with question-answer pairs that quote the context, alongside anchor tokens in a content-adaptive amount. Changing only the rehearsal lifts three hosts that score it in three different ways: Attic alone is the best training-free method in all eight settings we test on RULER and LongBench's natural-text tasks, and plugged into the gradient-based KVgrad and the trained RestoreKV+, it raises them by up to 17.1 and 28.1 points. Its advantage grows as the budget shrinks, reaching 41.9 points over full rereading at a 3% keep ratio, and on long documents it compresses faster than rereading them.

items.title: Dynamics as Code: On Model Compression via Dynamic System
items.description: arXiv:2610.11115v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The escalating size of pretrained neural networks has rendered model compression a prerequisite for deployment under stringent memory and compute constraints. With the irrational winding as an example, earlier work introduced a dynamic system (DS) paradigm that reconceptualizes compression as compact weight representation: high-dimensional parameters are encoded by the index of a trajectory produced by a dynamic system, from which the vector is recovered during decompression. This mechanism is fundamentally distinct from pruning, quantization, knowledge distillation, and low-rank decomposition. Along this direction, we prove that under a Diophantine condition, a finite trajectory of \(M = O(\epsilon^{-(d+\nu)})\) states in the irrational winding constitutes an \(\epsilon\)-net over the \(d\)-dimensional weight space, thereby linking state resolution, decompression error, and compression ratio in a predictable manner. Furthermore, we propose a generalized DS-based model compression framework by unifying four DS families---space-filling curves (Hilbert, Peano, Morton/Z-order, Snake), chaotic systems (Lorenz), congruential and pseudo-random generators (LCG, PCG), and low-discrepancy sequences (Halton). Also, we introduce the KD-tree and coordinate-template acceleration to scale to large models as well as outlier identification to control the error. Experiments on ResNet-18 and Qwen2.5-1.5B/Qwen1.5-7B validate that DS-based compression achieves competitive compression ratios without post-hoc retraining, with controllable decompression error and flexible state-space design, establishing it as a principled and practical compression approach.

items.title: When Do External Priors Help Low-Resource Structured Prediction? A Ranking-Level Alignment Study
items.description: arXiv:2610.11146v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Cold-start credit scoring (scarce labels, immature features, or minimal capacity) motivates injecting external priors (teacher models, LLMs, or domain experts) into training. We study Ranking Prior Alignment (RPA), a model-agnostic objective that aligns a model's ranking distribution to an external prior via a temperature-scaled KL loss with an annealed weight, $\mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}_{\text{task}} + \gamma(t)\,\text{KL}(P_{\text{agent}} \| P_{\text{model}})$, and requires no external model at inference. Across tree-ensemble and multiple-instance-learning (MIL) instantiations on the public Amex dataset and an industrial merchant-credit dataset (1.5M+ merchants), we ask when such priors genuinely transfer information rather than merely act as a regularizer. Our central finding: the prior's quality $\pi$ (its rank correlation with the label) governs transfer only when the alignment granularity matches the granularity at which $\pi$ is measured. On cross-sample tree alignment (Amex), a high-$\pi$ teacher yields $+0.028$ AUC over the no-alignment baseline (paired bootstrap 95% CI $[0.022, 0.035]$) whereas zero-information priors (uniform, random) yield none, and $\Delta$AUC tracks $\pi$ (XGBoost Pearson $r = 0.985$); this replicates on a second public dataset (LendingClub). On within-bag MIL-attention alignment, the same high-$\pi$ teacher transfers nothing: it is significantly worse than its own within-bag shuffle (net $-0.017$, 95% CI $< 0$, sign $p = 0.021$ over 10 seeds), while zero-information priors give the only significant gains: the KL term collapses to pure entropy regularization. We distill these results into a two-factor $N \cdot \mathcal{C}$ decision rule (gains concentrate at low sample size and capacity and vanish as either grows) and a scale-controlled paired protocol that separates information transfer from regularization.

items.title: When to Intervene? State-Aware Sparse Manipulation in Federated Reinforcement Learning
items.description: arXiv:2610.11523v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Federated reinforcement learning (FRL) enables distributed agents to collaboratively train decision-making policies, but its decentralized training process also exposes global policy learning to Byzantine manipulation. Existing poisoning attacks primarily focus on how to construct malicious updates, while trajectory-level intervention timing remains largely implicit. In sequential decision making, however, where an intervention is applied can alter subsequent trajectories and learning signals.
